Prebuilt **Linux and Windows x86-64** binaries of `k3`, the pure-C Kimi K3 inference
engine from [FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c](https://github.com/FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c),
built with the Tiny C Compiler (TCC) only.

**This is a Windows release.** It brings:

- faster loading on Windows;
- prompts, chat and file paths in any language;
- `setup.bat`, which builds k3 from source with one command.

The engine's output is unchanged from
[v1.2.2](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/releases/tag/v1.2.2), and Linux users get
the same engine. If you use k3 on Windows, upgrade.

## What changed on Windows

- **Much faster JSON parsing, so faster model loading.** Windows' C library
  (`msvcrt.dll`) scans the whole rest of the text every time it reads a number, which
  made k3's JSON parsing quadratic. k3 parses JSON for every safetensors header and for
  the 60 MB model index when it loads a model, and for its test fixtures. On a Windows CI
  runner, the test suite went from about **6.5 minutes to 9 seconds**. Numbers are now
  parsed from a short copy, which gives the same values on every platform.
- **Prompts and paths in any language.** Earlier builds received the command line and
  file names in the Windows "ANSI" code page, so most non-Latin text arrived as `?`.
  `k3.exe` now:
  - reads its command line as Unicode;
  - switches the console to UTF-8 for the run and restores it on exit;
  - reads typed chat input as Unicode;
  - opens, lists, renames and deletes files through the Unicode file APIs.

  `--prompt "..."` now works in Chinese, Arabic, emoji or any other script, and a model
  folder can have any name. `--prompt-file` still reads a file byte for byte.
- **`setup.bat`: one command from source to a tested `k3.exe`.** Clone the repository
  (or download its zip), then run `setup.bat`. It:
  - downloads the official TCC 0.9.27 and checks its SHA-256;
  - downloads TinyCC's source at the pinned commit (no `git` needed) and checks a
    SHA-256 over every file in it;
  - builds TCC 0.9.28rc;
  - builds k3 and runs the tests.

  Everything stays inside the repository folder. CI runs it on a fresh Windows machine
  on every push. See
  [docs/BUILD-WINDOWS.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.2.3/docs/BUILD-WINDOWS.md).
- **Thread pool hand-out.** Parallel loops now split into 4 blocks per thread, so a
  thread that wakes late still gets work. This mattered under Wine. On a real Windows
  runner the MXFP4 matmul scales 1.99x from 2 threads.

## Known difference between Windows and Linux

SiTU-GLU, ShortConv and the KDA decay use `expf` and `tanhf`. Windows' C library gives
slightly different results for these than glibc, so those three kernels are not
bit-identical across the two platforms. The matrix kernels, the KDA step and rmsnorm
are. Both platforms pass the reference tests. These three kernels are about 1% of a
token's compute.

## Also in this release

- **Checked on real weights (Linux).** The TCC build was run against four of the
  released shards (layers 0 and 1, embedding and head):
  - `test-all` passes;
  - the PyTorch comparison confirms every layer-1 binding at float32 rounding;
  - the expert bytes and dequantisation are identical;
  - tokenizer parity is 45/45.

  The full 93-layer model and Windows have not been run on real weights. Details are in
  [docs/TESTING.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.2.3/docs/TESTING.md).
- **Fixed:** `tools/verify_expert.py` crashed when run without arguments, because its
  default fixture path was wrong.
- **Release safety:** the release workflow now refuses a tag that does not match the
  source version, or that has no notes file, before building anything.
- **Benchmark:** `tcc -run build.c bench` now times every kernel and the thread pool,
  and CI runs it on Linux and Windows on every push.

## Speed

Unchanged from v1.2.2 on the same machine. The CI benchmark shows `windows-latest`
runners about 1.6-2.4x slower than `ubuntu-latest`, even for kernels that use no threads
and no C library. Linux and Windows TCC produce the same instructions for the hot loops,
and on one machine both builds run the matrix kernels at the same speed. That gap is the
runner hardware, not the Windows build.

## Downloads

| File | Runs on |
|---|---|
| `k3-1.2.3-windows-x64.zip` | 64-bit Windows Vista or later, any x86-64 CPU |
| `k3-1.2.3-linux-x64.zip` | 64-bit Linux with glibc 2.38 or newer (e.g. Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 39), any x86-64 CPU |
| `SHA256SUMS.txt` | Checksums for both zips |

Each zip contains `k3` (`k3.exe` on Windows), `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and `README.txt`.

- **No installer and no extra DLLs.**
  - `k3.exe` imports only `kernel32.dll` and `msvcrt.dll`.
  - The Linux `k3` needs only `libc.so.6` and `libm.so.6`.
- **Verify the download:**
  - PowerShell: `Get-FileHash .\k3-1.2.3-windows-x64.zip -Algorithm SHA256`
  - Linux: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing`
- **Quick check:** `k3 --version` should print `k3 1.2.3`.

Running inference needs the Kimi K3 checkpoint (about 1.56 TB), downloaded separately.
See [docs/QUICKSTART.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.2.3/docs/QUICKSTART.md).

## How it was built and verified

- **Build:** [`release.yml`](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.2.3/.github/workflows/release.yml)
  on GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` and `windows-latest` runners, with TCC 0.9.28rc (TinyCC
  commit `e23dabed`).
- **Tests before packaging:** the full weightless suite ran on each OS, with these
  results: `22 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped`, `VERDICT: ENGINE MATCHES THE REFERENCE
  EXACTLY` and `ALL WEIGHTLESS TESTS PASSED`. The new Unicode test passed on real Windows
  too, including the command-line round trip.
- **Output unchanged:** the matrix-kernel output digests match v1.2.2. `test_ops` passes
  at 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 threads, and the full-model oracle at 1, 3 and 8.
- **Not verified:** inference on real Kimi K3 weights on Windows, and the full 93-layer
  model on any platform.

Full history: [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.2.3/CHANGELOG.md).
